messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: UX Designer
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Vignette:
Kofi Mensah is a 19-year-old Ghanaian-American UX designer who recently completed a remote internship and was beginning to build what looked, from the outside, like a promising early career. He presents to therapy with a PCL-5 score of 65, referred by his university's counselling service after a resident advisor noticed he had stopped attending in-person classes entirely.

The stalking began approximately eight months ago, during the final weeks of his freshman year. Kofi had met another student through a shared design forum, and what started as enthusiastic messages about typography and interface work gradually shifted in register. The messages came faster, arrived at unusual hours, and began referencing details — what he had been wearing in the campus library, which coffee shop he had visited that afternoon — that made clear he was being watched without his knowledge. When Kofi responded less frequently, attempting to create distance, the contact escalated. The individual began appearing outside his dormitory. One evening, returning from a late studio session, Kofi found a handwritten note slipped under his door that described, in precise detail, the route he had walked home. He stood in his doorway for a long time that night, holding the note, understanding that someone had been close enough to follow him step for step and he had not noticed.

He had come to believe, in the months that followed, that he had brought this on himself. He had been friendly on the forum. He had replied to messages. He had, as he put it in his first session, "acted like someone worth following." This conviction — that his own openness had functioned as an invitation — settled into him quietly but with considerable weight. He does not describe it as guilt exactly, more as a kind of retrospective certainty that he had misread the situation and paid for it.

What he carries most visibly now is the sense that the world is a place where danger assembles itself without announcement. He had grown up trusting that ordinary public spaces operated by legible rules; that belief did not survive the note under his door. He is certain that safety is provisional at best, that any environment can conceal someone watching, and that the appropriate response to this is permanent alertness. He checks the area around his apartment building before he exits. He varies his walking routes, though he could not always explain the logic of the variation. On video calls for his UX work — the remote position he took specifically because it required no commute, no fixed public schedule — he positions his camera so that the background reveals nothing identifiable about where he is.

His work has not collapsed, but it has narrowed. He was invited to attend a design sprint in person at the company's offices last month and declined, offering a vague excuse about scheduling. His supervisor followed up twice. Kofi did not respond to either message. He is aware that this silence will have consequences and finds himself unable to close the gap. The idea of walking through an unfamiliar building, through corridors he has not mapped, among people whose presence he cannot account for, is not something he can currently organise himself to do. His professional life is now conducted entirely through a screen, from a single room, with the door locked.

He has not told his family in detail what happened. His mother calls weekly and he answers, keeping his voice level. He has not explained why he no longer visits the campus design lab he once spoke about with enthusiasm, or why the group chat with his two closest friends from the dorm has gone unanswered for three months. The friendships have not formally ended; they have simply gone quiet, the way a room goes quiet when no one enters it.

What finally brought him to the counselling service was not a crisis but an accumulation. He had been sitting at his desk one evening, working on a wireframe, and realised he had spent forty minutes listening to the hallway outside his door rather than working. He described this moment in intake as the point at which he understood something had to change. What he is most afraid of, he said, is that it already has — permanently. What he is hoping for, more tentatively, is some evidence that he is wrong about that.
